Literal Sense

The Setting: Abraham's Journey to Gerar

Genesis 20 opens with Abraham's departure from Mamre following the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah: "Abraham removed from thence to the south country, and dwelt between Cades and Sur, and sojourned in Gerara" (Gen 20:1). The patriarch, now approaching his hundredth year, journeys into the territory of the Philistines, specifically to Gerar, a city ruled by King Abimelech. This geographical movement places Abraham in foreign territory where he perceives himself to be vulnerable.

Abraham's Deception

Upon arriving in Gerar, Abraham employs the same strategy he had used decades earlier in Egypt: "And he said of Sara his wife: She is my sister. So Abimelech the king of Gerara sent, and took her" (Gen 20:2). This deception, while technically a half-truth since Sarah was indeed his half-sister, was intended to protect Abraham from being killed by those who might desire his beautiful wife.

St. Augustine, in his treatise Against Lying, carefully analyzes Abraham's statement:

"He did not say, She is not my wife, but he said, She is my sister; because she was in truth so near akin, that she might without a lie be called a sister. He left untold the truth about her being his wife, but told of sister; he did not speak a falsehood."

St. Augustine, Contra Mendacium (Against Lying)

Augustine further explains in The City of God that Abraham "called his wife his sister, and told no lie. For she was this also, because she was near of blood." He notes that Abraham "held his peace" about her marital status while "committing to God the defense of his wife's chastity, and providing as a man against human wiles."

Divine Intervention: God's Warning to Abimelech

The narrative takes a dramatic turn when God Himself intervenes to protect Sarah: "And God came to Abimelech in a dream by night, and he said to him: Lo thou shalt die for the woman that thou hast taken: for she hath a husband" (Gen 20:3). This divine warning through a dream represents one of the earliest instances of God communicating with a pagan ruler to protect His covenant purposes.

Abimelech protests his innocence: "Lord, wilt thou slay a nation that is ignorant and just? Did not he say to me: She is my sister: and she say, He is my brother? In the simplicity of my heart, and cleanness of my hands have I done this" (Gen 20:4-5). God acknowledges the king's integrity: "I know that thou didst it with a sincere heart: and therefore I withheld thee from sinning against me, and I suffered thee not to touch her" (Gen 20:6).

St. Augustine, in Book XVI of The City of God, comments on this episode:

"Then Abraham did again at Gerar, with Abimelech the king of that city, what he had done in Egypt about his wife, and received her back untouched in the same way. Her beauty was so great that even at that advanced age she could be fallen in love with."

St. Augustine, City of God, XVI.30

Abraham Declared a Prophet

In this passage, Abraham receives for the first time in Scripture the title of prophet: "Now therefore restore the man his wife, for he is a prophet: and he shall pray for thee, and thou shalt live" (Gen 20:7). This is the first occurrence of the Hebrew word nabiy (prophet) in the Bible, and it is connected specifically with intercessory prayer.

The prophetic office here is understood primarily in terms of intercession. As one early commentator observed: "The proper meaning of the Hebrew nabi is to pray, entreat, make supplication. As those who were in habits of intimacy with God through prayer and faith were found most suitable to communicate His mind to man, the intercessor became in time the public instructor and predictor of future events."

Abraham's Explanation

When confronted by Abimelech, Abraham offers a revealing explanation for his conduct: "I thought with myself, saying: Perhaps there is not the fear of God in this place: and they will kill me for the sake of my wife" (Gen 20:11). He then clarifies the family relationship: "Howbeit, otherwise also she is truly my sister, the daughter of my father, and not the daughter of my mother, and I took her to wife" (Gen 20:12).

St. John Chrysostom, in his Homilies on Genesis, emphasizes the theme of divine providence throughout this narrative:

"Consider, I ask you, those who have been pleasing to the Lord from the beginning up to the present time... no longer consider the thing to be impossible, nor be apathetic where virtue is concerned, but accept such opportunities as the Lord leaves for laying hold of virtue with ease."

St. John Chrysostom, Homilies on Genesis, 45

Resolution and Blessing

The chapter concludes with Abimelech restoring Sarah to Abraham along with generous gifts: "And Abimelech took sheep and oxen, and servants and handmaids, and gave to Abraham: and restored to him Sara his wife" (Gen 20:14). Abimelech also grants Abraham permission to dwell anywhere in his land and provides a thousand pieces of silver as a vindication of Sarah's honor.

The narrative ends with Abraham's intercessory prayer: "And when Abraham prayed, God healed Abimelech and his wife, and his handmaids, and they bore children" (Gen 20:17). This healing prayer demonstrates the prophetic ministry of intercession and establishes a pattern that will continue throughout Scripture.
allegorical:
Allegorical Sense

Abraham and Christ: The Pattern of Divine Protection

The allegorical reading of Genesis 20 reveals profound typological connections between Abraham's experience and the mysteries of Christ and His Church. Just as Abraham journeyed through foreign lands while God protected his household, so Christ descended into the world, a foreign territory corrupted by sin, while the Father preserved His mission and His Bride, the Church.

St. Irenaeus of Lyons, in his Against Heresies, establishes the foundational principle for reading Abraham's story Christologically:

"Since, therefore, Abraham was a prophet and saw in the Spirit the day of the Lord's coming, and the dispensation of His suffering, through whom both he himself and all who, following the example of his faith, trust in God, should be saved, he rejoiced exceedingly... For faith towards God justifies a man."

St. Irenaeus of Lyons, Against Heresies, IV.7

Sarah as the Church

In patristic allegorical interpretation, Sarah consistently represents the Church, the Bride of Christ. Her temporary captivity in Abimelech's household and subsequent deliverance prefigures the Church's experience in the world. Though she dwells among those who do not know her true identity and worth, she remains protected by divine providence and is ultimately restored to her rightful place.

St. Ambrose of Milan, in his treatise On Abraham, develops this allegorical framework:

"Abraham represents the mind. In fact, Abraham signifies passage. Therefore, in order that the mind, which in Adam had allowed itself to run to pleasure and to bodily attractions, should turn toward the ideal form of virtue, a wise man has been proposed to us as an example to imitate."

St. Ambrose of Milan, On Abraham, I

The Apostle Paul's allegorization of Sarah in Galatians 4:21-31 provides the apostolic foundation for this reading. Sarah represents the free woman, the mother of the children of promise, the heavenly Jerusalem. Her protection in Gerar foreshadows the divine preservation of the Church throughout her pilgrimage in this world.

The Dream as Divine Revelation

God's appearance to Abimelech in a dream demonstrates that divine revelation extends beyond the covenant community. This prefigures the universal mission of the Gospel, whereby God speaks to all nations and calls all peoples to repentance. Abimelech, though a pagan king, responds with integrity to divine revelation, anticipating the Gentiles who would receive the Gospel with faith.

St. Justin Martyr, though writing primarily about Abraham's earlier encounter with divine visitors, articulates the principle that applies here:

"Therefore neither Abraham, nor Isaac, nor Jacob, nor any other man, saw the Father and ineffable Lord of all, and also of Christ, but saw Him who was according to His will His Son, being God, and the Angel because He ministered to His will."

St. Justin Martyr, Dialogue with Trypho, 127

The Wife-Sister Mystery

The peculiar circumstance of Sarah being both wife and sister to Abraham carries deep allegorical significance. The Church is both Bride and Sister to Christ. As Bride, she is united to Him in the mystery of divine espousal; as Sister, she shares His nature through the Incarnation, whereby He became our Brother by assuming human flesh. The double relationship points to the intimate union between Christ and His Church that operates on multiple levels.

Origen, the great Alexandrian exegete, developed such dual interpretations extensively. In his Homilies on Genesis, he explains how Sarah represents virtue and wisdom, which belongs properly to the soul united to Christ:

"The bride is the Church. On the psychological level she is the soul. In either case the Bridegroom is the Logos."

Origen, Commentary on the Song of Songs

Abraham as Prophet and Intercessor

Abraham's designation as a prophet in this chapter prefigures Christ's prophetic office. More specifically, Abraham's role as intercessor who prays for Abimelech's household points to Christ's eternal intercession for His people: "He is able also to save for ever them that come to God by him; always living to make intercession for us" (Heb 7:25).

The healing that comes through Abraham's prayer anticipates the healing that flows from Christ to all who call upon His name. As Abraham stood between Abimelech and divine judgment, pleading for mercy, so Christ stands between sinful humanity and the Father as our eternal advocate.

The Seed of Promise Protected

The entire episode ultimately concerns the protection of the promised seed. Sarah, who will soon conceive Isaac, must be preserved from defilement so that the covenant promise might be fulfilled through her. This points forward to the preservation of Mary's virginity and the protection of the Incarnation itself. God guards the vessels through which His promises are fulfilled.

St. Cyril of Alexandria emphasizes how Christ is the true Seed of Abraham:

"'He has remembered His mercy as He promised to Abraham:' and has accomplished what He spake unto him, that 'in thy seed shall all the tribes of the earth be blessed.' For this promise was now in the act of fulfilment by the impending birth of our common Saviour Christ, Who is that seed of Abraham, in Whom the Gentiles are blessed."

St. Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke
moral:
Moral Sense

The Fear of God as Foundation of Morality

Genesis 20 introduces a concept that pervades all of Scripture: the fear of God as the foundation of moral conduct. Abraham's explanation for his deception is revealing: "I thought with myself, saying: Perhaps there is not the fear of God in this place" (Gen 20:11). This phrase, "the fear of God," appears here for the first time in connection with ethical behavior and establishes a principle that the wisdom literature will later develop extensively: "The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom" (Prov 9:10).

The fear of God, as the Church Fathers understood it, is not servile terror but reverential awe that shapes moral character. St. Augustine distinguishes different types of fear:

"The fear of God not only begins but also perfects wisdom, whereby we love God above all things, and our neighbor as ourselves."

St. Augustine

St. Thomas Aquinas further develops this teaching in the Summa Theologica:

"If a man turn to God and adhere to Him, through fear of punishment, it will be servile fear; but if it be on account of fear of committing a fault, it will be filial fear, for it becomes a child to fear offending its father."

St. Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologica, II-II, Q.19

The Danger of Presumption

Abraham's presumption that there was no fear of God in Gerar proved to be mistaken. Ironically, it was the pagan king Abimelech who demonstrated greater moral sensitivity in this episode than the patriarch himself. This teaches us not to assume that those outside our community lack moral integrity or divine guidance.

One commentator observes the profound irony: "The irony is, in this story, if there is anyone who lacks the fear of God it would be Abraham himself. Indeed, Abraham has miscalculated the situation and so has resorted to his own use of deceitful tactics and schemes. It is the pagan king Abimelech who is the voice of divine rebuke to Abraham."

Victor Hamilton notes that God's people need to learn that they "do not have a monopoly on revelation" from God, that "the revelation of His will to all people is possible." This humbling lesson challenges presumption and calls for humility in our dealings with those outside the visible community of faith.

The Ethics of Truth-Telling

Abraham's half-truth raises complex questions about the ethics of deception. While technically accurate, his statement that Sarah was his sister was intended to deceive and thus partook of the nature of a lie. St. Augustine addresses this directly:

"It is not then a lie, when by silence a true thing is kept back, but when by speech a false thing is put forward."

St. Augustine, Contra Mendacium

Yet Augustine's careful distinction also implicitly critiques Abraham's approach. While Abraham did not explicitly lie, he created a false impression with the intent to deceive. The moral lesson is that integrity requires not merely the avoidance of explicit falsehood but truthfulness in our overall communication. A half-truth spoken with intent to deceive participates in the malice of lying even if it escapes its technical definition.

The Virtue of Integrity

Abimelech emerges as a surprising moral exemplar in this narrative. He acts with what he calls "the simplicity of my heart, and cleanness of my hands" (Gen 20:5), and God Himself confirms this assessment. When confronted with divine revelation, Abimelech responds immediately with obedience, restoring Sarah and seeking reconciliation.

St. John Chrysostom frequently held up such examples of pagan virtue to challenge his Christian audience:

"Our loving Lord, knowing the weakness of our purpose and our tendency to fall, has left us great remedies in the reading of the Scriptures so that we might constantly apply them to ourselves and recall the lives of those great and wonderful men."

St. John Chrysostom, Homilies on Genesis

The Power of Intercessory Prayer

Abraham's designation as a prophet is directly connected to his ministry of intercession. God commands Abimelech to seek Abraham's prayer, establishing the principle that the prayers of the righteous have special efficacy. This passage, containing the first use of "prophet" in Scripture, also contains the first mention of "prayer" (palal in Hebrew), linking prophecy and intercession from the very beginning.

The moral obligation to pray for others, even for those who have wronged us or stand under divine judgment, is thus established. Abraham had been wronged by Abimelech's taking of Sarah, yet he is commanded to pray for the king's household. This prefigures our Lord's command: "Love your enemies: do good to them that hate you: and pray for them that persecute and calumniate you" (Matt 5:44).

Divine Providence and Human Weakness

The chapter reveals how God works through human weakness to accomplish His purposes. Abraham's faith faltered; he resorted to deception out of fear. Yet God protected the covenant promise despite the patriarch's moral failure. This teaches us both the gravity of sin and the superabundance of divine grace.

Gregory of Nyssa reflects on how Abraham serves as a model despite his imperfections:

"Consider Abraham your father, and Sarah who gave you birth. Scripture gives this admonition to those who wander outside virtue. Just as at sea those who are carried away from the direction of the harbor bring themselves back on course by a clear sign... in the same way Scripture by the example of Abraham and Sarah may guide again to the harbor of the divine will those adrift on the sea of life."

St. Gregory of Nyssa, Life of Moses

The Vulnerability of the Righteous

Abraham's fear for his life reminds us that the righteous are not exempt from danger in this world. The just must often live among those who do not share their values, and this creates genuine vulnerability. Yet the proper response to such vulnerability is trust in divine providence, not deception. As the Psalmist declares: "The Lord is my light and my salvation, whom shall I fear?" (Ps 26:1).
anagogical:
Anagogical Sense

The Church's Pilgrimage Among the Nations

Genesis 20, read anagogically, illuminates the Church's eschatological journey through history toward her eternal homeland. Abraham's sojourn in Gerar, a foreign land where he feared there was no fear of God, prefigures the Church's pilgrimage through the present age. Like Sarah, the Bride of Christ dwells among those who do not recognize her true identity, yet she is preserved by divine providence for the day of her full manifestation.

St. Irenaeus articulates the eschatological hope that animates this pilgrimage:

"Along with Abraham shall we inherit the holy land, when we shall receive the inheritance for an endless eternity, being children of Abraham through the like faith."

St. Irenaeus of Lyons, Against Heresies, V.32

Divine Preservation Until the End

Just as God protected Sarah from defilement in Abimelech's household, so He preserves His Church from ultimate corruption until the end of time. The gates of hell shall not prevail against her (Matt 16:18). Though she may be taken captive by the powers of this world, though her true nature may be hidden or misunderstood, she remains inviolate, awaiting the day of her full vindication.

The early Church understood herself as living in history's final age, constantly facing the end. Brian Daley observes in his study of patristic eschatology that the Church Fathers reflected a "sense of constantly living in history's final age, of facing, amid persecutions and natural disasters, the end of society." This eschatological consciousness shapes the reading of narratives like Genesis 20.

God's Warning Dream and the Final Judgment

God's warning to Abimelech in a dream carries anagogical significance. The divine communication that came to the pagan king prefigures the universal revelation that will accompany the final judgment, when every conscience will be laid bare before God. "For nothing is covered that shall not be revealed: nor hid, that shall not be known" (Matt 10:26).

Abimelech's response to divine warning models the proper human response to eschatological revelation: immediate repentance and restitution. Those who, like Abimelech, respond to divine warning with integrity of heart will find mercy; those who harden their hearts against such warning face the severity of divine judgment.

Abraham's Bosom and Eternal Rest

Abraham himself becomes in later Scripture a symbol of eschatological rest. The poor man Lazarus is carried by angels to "Abraham's bosom" (Luke 16:22), a phrase that the Church Fathers interpreted as signifying the blessed state of the righteous after death.

The Catholic Encyclopedia explains this patristic understanding:

"In patristic literature it often means heaven. It implies a return of Abraham's spiritual descendants to the embrace of the earthly father of all the faithful."

Catholic Encyclopedia, "The Bosom of Abraham"

St. Augustine likewise referred to "the righteous dead as disembodied spirits blissfully awaiting Judgment Day in secret receptacles." The narrative of Genesis 20, with its theme of divine protection and ultimate restoration, points toward this blessed rest that awaits all who share Abraham's faith.

The Restoration of All Things

The chapter's conclusion, with Sarah restored to Abraham and the households healed through his intercession, prefigures the final restoration of all things. What was taken will be restored; what was afflicted will be healed; what was separated will be reunited. This is the eschatological hope that pervades the entire biblical narrative.

The healing of Abimelech's household through Abraham's prayer anticipates the healing of the nations that will occur when Christ returns. "God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes: and death shall be no more, nor mourning, nor crying, nor sorrow shall be any more" (Rev 21:4). The intercessory prayer of Abraham prefigures Christ's eternal intercession, which sustains the world until the fullness of time.

The Heavenly Jerusalem

Sarah, as a type of the Church and of the heavenly Jerusalem (Gal 4:26), points beyond herself to the eschatological reality. Her sojourn in Gerar, a city of the Philistines, represents the Church's temporary dwelling in the earthly city. Her restoration to Abraham anticipates the Church's final gathering to Christ at His coming.

Tertullian, reflecting on the early Christian hope, wrote of the heavenly Jerusalem:

"We do confess that a kingdom is promised to us upon the earth, although before heaven, only in another state of existence; in as much as it will be after the resurrection for a thousand years in the divinely-built city of Jerusalem."

Tertullian, Against Marcion

The Fear of God Perfected in Love

Abraham's concern about the absence of the fear of God in Gerar finds its eschatological resolution in the perfection of that fear in the age to come. The fear of God, which begins as reverential awe and develops into filial love, will be perfected in the beatific vision when we see God face to face. Then all fear of punishment will be cast out, and only the pure fear of love will remain.

St. John writes: "Fear is not in charity: but perfect charity casteth out fear, because fear hath pain. And he that feareth, is not perfected in charity" (1 John 4:18). The anagogical reading of Genesis 20 points toward this eschatological perfection of love, when the fear that Abraham found lacking in Gerar will be fulfilled in the eternal worship of the heavenly Jerusalem.

The Prophet's Intercession and Final Salvation

Abraham's role as prophet-intercessor reaches its eschatological fulfillment in Christ's eternal high priesthood. The temporary healing that came through Abraham's prayer is a shadow of the eternal salvation that comes through Christ's intercession. He "is able also to save for ever them that come to God by him; always living to make intercession for us" (Heb 7:25).

This intercession continues until the last day, when the number of the elect is complete and Christ returns to judge the living and the dead. Until that day, the Church lives under the protection of her Bridegroom's constant prayer, preserved like Sarah for the day of her full glorification.
